title: TB8-14425
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX XXXX (the Appellant) is a Kurdish citizen of Iraq. He appealed a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD), dated December 4, 2017, rejecting his claim for refugee protection. The Appellant alleges he faces persecution and a risk to life stemming from a business dispute he had with the Chavy Land Group, whom he alleges has political affiliations. The determinative issue in this case for the RPD was credibility.
I agree with the RPD that the Appellant has not credibly established his allegation. For the reasons that follow, the appeal is dismissed.

The Appellant alleges that he started a restaurant and entered into a rental agreement with the Chavy Land group. He alleges that the Chavy Land Group attempted to unilaterally change the terms of the rental agreement. He alleges that when he complained about their actions they began threatening him and his family. The Appellant alleges that he filed a complaint with the courts and with the police, but nothing came of these efforts. The Appellant also alleges that he sought assistance from members of the business community to resolve his dispute but was unsuccessful. The Appellant alleges that he was unable to get justice because the Chavy Land group has connections with influential individuals. He alleges that the owner of this group also owns a media company (NTR) and is now a politician with influence in Kurdistan. As such, the Appellant fears that he and his family would be harmed in order to serve as an example of what would happen to people who oppose this political party.

The Appellant travelled to Canada on two occasions in 2016 but did not initiate a refugee claim as he alleges at that time he was still attempting to get justice in Iraq. The Appellant alleges that after his wife and children were threatened, he decided they were no longer safe and the family moved to Jordan where they registered claims with the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR). The Appellant alleges that his family did not feel safe in Jordan so they moved to Turkey and transferred their claims to the UNHCR in Turkey. He alleges that they faced a significant wait time before their claims would be assessed and therefore he decided to utilize his Canadian visa and travelled to Canada in XXXX 2017.

The RPD concluded that the Appellant's allegations were not credibly established. The RPD also considered his residual profile and found that the Appellant did not face a serious possibility of persecution or a risk to life.

The Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) reviews decisions of the RPD on a standard of correctness after conducting an independent assessment of the evidence before it. The exception to this rule is where the RPD enjoys a meaningful advantage in the assessment and weighing of oral testimony heard, which in particular cases, attracts deference. Unless specifically stated below, I have applied a correctness standard.1 ANALYSIS Appellant's arguments
paragraphs.heading_before: ROLE OF THE REFUGEE APPEAL DIVISION

paragraphs.text: The Appellant argue that the RPD erred in its credibility assessment. Specifically, the Appellant argues that the inconsistencies referenced by the RPD are not supported by the record. The Appellant also argues that the RPD erred by not accepting his explanation for his failure to claim on previous trips to Canada. The Appellant argues that he has established he faces persecution and a risk to life in Iraq. The Appellant also submits new evidence with his appeal.

Section 110(4) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA)2 sets out that an appellant may only present evidence that arose after the rejection of their claim, or that was not reasonably available, or that they could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented at the time of the rejection. Where evidence meets the requirements of section 110(4), the RAD will then go on to consider the factors affirmed by the Federal Court of Appeal in Singh.3

The Appellant has submitted a number of documents as new evidence with his appeal. He has submitted an affidavit from someone who claims to have been a witness to one of the threats that were made against him as well as a statement from his wife. He has also submitted a document purported to be from the court in Sulaymaniyah, Iraq and three news articles. The Affidavit of XXXX XXXX XXXX will not be admitted

The affidavit submitted as new evidence is from an individual (XXXX XXXX XXXX) who alleges he witnessed the Appellant being threatened by XXXX XXXX XXXX. I find that this affidavit does not meet the requirements set out in 110(4) of the IRPA. The content of the affidavit is not new as it relates to the threats that were central to the basis of the Appellant's claim.

The RAD notes that Rule 3(3)(g) of the RAD Rules requires the Appellant's memorandum include among other things, full and detailed submissions regarding: (iii) how any documentary evidence referred to in paragraph (e) meets the requirements of subsection 110(4) of the Act and how that evidence relates to the appellant4 The Appellant offers no real explanation as to why this affidavit was not presented to the RPD. The Appellant's memo states "At the time of the rejection of the claim, no evidence was available to the Claimant/Appellant. So he is providing an affidavit from a neighbouring business owner to address this issue."5 Aside from this vague statement, the Appellant has failed to establish why this evidence was unavailable to him before the rejection of his claim.

I find that it would be reasonable to expect that the Appellant would have provided this information to the RPD as it is directly related to the matter at the heart of his claim. The burden is on claimants to establish their allegations before the RPD. The Court has held: [14] ... that the Applicant must put her best foot forward before the RPD, and present all the evidence that is available at the time, whether aware of it or not, unless there is an aspect of injustice arising from unexpected new facts, or old facts that no reasonable amount of due diligence could have turned up. It is not intended to be a tune-up procedure for the RAD that upon learning in deficiencies in the Applicant's case, additional evidence that could have been presented to the RPD may be presented as new evidence before the RAD. [15] In other words, responding to an inadequacy identified by the RPD in a party's case cannot be a legitimate foundation for the party to claim that had she known about the deficiency she could have presented better evidence that was always in existence from persons that could have been called, in this case from her cousin. This would make the RPD process a monumental waste of time, which is surely not Parliament's intention in providing appeal rights.6

I find that the Appellant has not established how this evidence meets the requirements of section 110(4) of the IRPA. As such, I will not go on to assess the factors affirmed by the Federal Court of Appeal in Singh. The statement of the Appellant's wife will not be admitted

The Appellant has submitted a statement from his wife outlining the details of the alleged threat made against her and their children which prompted the Appellant not to return to Iraq. This statement suffers from many of the same deficiencies as the affidavit from XXXX XXXX XXXX. The information in the statement is not new as it relates to the threat that the Appellant alleges occurred before he made a refugee claim in Canada. Once again, I find that that this evidence is related to the central element of the Appellant's allegation, specifically that his family was threatened by representatives of the Chavy Land group. This specific incident was the alleged catalyst for the Appellant to seek protection outside of Iraq. As such, I find that the Appellant ought to have presented this evidence to the RPD.

The Appellant argues that the evidence was not previously available to him because "At the time of the Appeal and before that, the Appellant's wife did not have a stable home and did not have any place to live with their children. She had no access to a computer and nobody else was helping her at that time. So, her affidavit is a very important evidence that Appellant wants to present for his appeal."7 I find that this statement does not establish why the evidence was not available to the Appellant in some form. Even accepting that the Appellant's wife did not have access to a computer, there has been no explanation as to why she could not have presented this evidence in a hand-written letter or by being a witness at the RPD by telephone. Therefore, I find that the Appellant has not established how this statement meets the requirements of section 110(4) of the IRPA. The news articles will not be accepted

The Appellant has submitted three articles about the activities of Chavy land group. These articles are dated October 26, 2013, November 20, 2017 and June 28, 2016. I find that the Appellant has not established that these articles meet the requirement of 110(4) of the IRPA. The Appellant offers no explanation about why they were not presented to the RPD before the Appellant's claim was rejected on December 4, 2017. The Appellant simply states that the documents are very important. Again, I note that the Appellant, who is represented by counsel, must establish how the new evidence submitted meets the requirements to be admitted. There is no indication why the Appellant did not submit these documents to the RPD given that they were clearly related to the heart of his claim, as they reference the alleged activities of Chavy Land company. Given that these articles were published prior to the rejection of the claim, and absent any explanation as to why they were unavailable, I find that they do not meet the requirements of section 110(4) of the IRPA and I will therefore not consider the factors in Singh. The court document will not be accepted

The Appellant submitted a document that he purports is from the Provincial Court in Iraq. In considering the requirements of 110(4), I find that the document was not available to the Appellant at the time of the rejection of his claim. Although the Appellant failed to articulate when he obtained this document, I have independently reviewed the record and note that his inability to obtain the court documents was discussed at his RPD hearing. The Appellant testified that he had asked his lawyer to obtain the documents for him but that obtaining this record from the court was taking a significant amount of time. The Appellant testified that he would continue to try and obtain this document.8 Therefore, accepting the Appellant's testimony I find that this document would not have been available to him prior to the rejection of his claim.

In applying the Singh factors, I find that the document is not admissible as it is not credible. In reviewing the document and comparing it to other evidence on the record, I find that there are issues with this document that render it not credible. The translated version indicates that the claimant is "XXXX XXXX XXXX"9. However, according to the Appellant's Basis of Claim (BOC) and associated forms his name is XXXX XXXX XXXX. This is also how his name is listed later on in this same court document. The inconsistencies with the name of the Appellant raise concerns with the credibility of the document.

Further, the document indicates that the respondent is "chevy land company;" however in all the other evidence, including the Appellant's BOC narrative10 and the rental agreement11 he submitted to the RPD the landlord is listed as the "Chavy Land". This discrepancy raises a further concern with the document's credibility.

Finally, a review of the content of the document reveals that the information in it is in direct contradiction with the other evidence on the record. These contradictions in the content of the document are the most significant factor in my determination that this document is not credible. The court document indicates that the complaint is based on: Chevy Land of using illegal ways to terminate the agreement and for this reason. 1- I am asking the honorable court to investigate with the respondent and find a reasonable justify solution for those signed contracts between us. 2- Stopping the threats and protection for me and solve the matter with a legal ways. This is in contradiction with the Appellant's other evidence that the dispute was related to the Chavy Land group increasing his rent and changing the terms of the rental agreement from five to two years.12 There is no indication that the landlord was attempting to terminate the lease as outlined in this document. This is also in direct contradiction with his evidence before the RPD that the court complaint was about the landlord's attempt to change the rental agreement without his consent.13 Further, the Appellant's evidence before the RPD was that he was first threatened in February 2016.14 In his BOC narrative he indicates he was first threatened in March 2016.15 However this court document is dated July 2015 and references threats received by the Appellant, long before the Appellant alleges any threats occurred.16 Given all these contradictions, I find that the court document is not credible and does not meet the factors in Singh. Credibility There are contradictions about when the threats started and the nature of the threats

The RPD found that the Appellant's testimony about when threats against him began was in contradiction with his BOC narrative. Specifically, the RPD found that in his narrative the Appellant indicated that he was first threatened in March 2016 while in testimony he indicated that he was threatened in February 2016. The RPD found that this was a significant inconsistency which undermined his credibility.

The Appellant argues that there is no such contradiction in his evidence. He argues that his BOC narrative references discussions he had with representative of the Chavy Land Group in February 2016 and that this is in fact consistent with his testimony.

Having independently reviewed the record, I agree with the RPD. While I agree that the Appellant referenced a discussion he had with representatives of Chavy Land in February 2016 in his BOC, he does not mention any threats. The first mention of any threats in the Appellant's narrative is that "In March 2016, Chavy Land representatives approached me again. This time, they threatened me by saying that if I don't stop what I was doing my life and my family's lives would come to an end."17 In his testimony, the Appellant claimed that the first threat he received was in February 201618. I agree with the RPD that there is a discrepancy in the Appellant's evidence about when he was first threatened. The Appellant was asked about this discrepancy and did not provide an explanation, simply restating that the threats began in February 2016.19 Given these threats are central to the Appellant's claim, I find this contradiction impugns the credibility of the Appellant's allegation.

The RPD also found that there was a significant omission in the Appellant's evidence about the nature of the threats he received. Specifically, the RPD noted that the Appellant testified that he was threatened by men who were armed with guns in July 2016 but did not mention this in his BOC narrative. The RPD found that this was a significant omission that was directly related to the heart of his claim.

The Appellant makes no argument about this finding in his memorandum. I have independently reviewed the record and I agree with the RPD. I find that this is a significant omission related to a very important aspect of the Appellant's claim. The Appellant was asked about this omission and he testified that his head was clearer after the passage of time.20 I also agree with the RPD that the Appellant's explanation for this omission is not credible. Given the significance of this event to establishing the Appellant's allegation that he feared for his life at the hands of the Chavy land group, I find that the omission of this information undermines the credibility of the allegation. The details about the Appellant's contact with the police are inconsistent.

The RPD found that the Appellant's testimony about when and how he contacted the police was inconsistent with what was in his BOC narrative. The RPD noted that the Appellant testified that his first contact with the police was when he attended the police station in person after his restaurant was emptied21, however his BOC narrative indicated he called them when this occurred. When asked about this inconsistency, the Appellant testified that he first called the police then attended the station. When asked why this was not outlined in his BOC, he testified that the events happened a long time ago and it was hard to recall given his age.22 The RPD noted that the Appellant was only 42 years old and there was no evidence to suggest he faced any cognitive issues that would impact his memory. As such, the RPD did not accept the Appellant's explanation and found this inconsistency undermined the credibility of the allegation.

The RPD also found that the Appellant's testimony regarding what the police said to him about why they would not assist him was inconsistent. The RPD noted that the Appellant testified that when he spoke with police after the restaurant was emptied they told him that they could not assist him and that he should go through the courts.23 However, in his BOC narrative, the Appellant indicated that the police told him that they could not assist him because the matter was "connected to higher officials"24. Further, the RPD noted that although the Appellant testified that he reported the threats against him to the police twice,25 he does not mention this in his BOC narrative. The RPD found that these further inconsistencies undermined the credibility of the Appellant's allegation.

The Appellant argues that the RPD erred by finding there were inconsistencies. Although the argument is not very clear, the Appellant essentially contends that he has consistently maintained that he went to the police and they did not help him.

Having reviewed the record, I agree with the RPD. I find that the Appellant's evidence about how he contacted the police and what their response was following the emptying of his restaurant has been inconsistent. I also agree that the Appellant's evidence about whether he reported the threats against him to the police has been inconsistent. I find that the Appellant failed to provide a reasonable explanation for these inconsistencies, and as such they impugn the credibility of his allegation. The Appellant's failure to claim during his previous trips to Canada further impugn the credibility of his allegation

The RPD found that the Appellant's failure to make a refugee claim when he travelled to Canada in XXXX and XXXX 2016 further diminishes the veracity of his allegations. The RPD noted that these trips occurred after the Appellant was allegedly threatened by the Chavy Land group. The RPD found that if the Appellant had really been threatened and told by the police that they could not help him, he would have made a refugee claim during these two trips.

The Appellant argues that he did not make a claim on his previous trips to Canada as he was trying to recover the money he had lost in this dispute. The Appellant also states that "he is providing a statement to address this issue"26 I would note that the Appellant's statement for the purposes of an appeal is not the way in which he can introduce new evidence. I have reviewed the statement and it simply re-iterates the Appellant's explanation that he did not advance a claim on his previous trips as he hoped to recover the savings he had invested in the restaurant.

In independently considering the record before me, I agree with the RPD that the Appellant's failure to claim on his trips to Canada impugns the credibility of his allegation that he had been threatened by representatives of Chavy Land. While I can accept that the Appellant had a desire to recover the money he lost in his business venture, I find that this does not explain his failure to claim. The Appellant alleges he was threatened once or twice before his trip in April. He also alleges that he was threatened by armed men prior to his second trip and that he knew these individuals were connected and that the police would not help him. Despite this, he did not advance a refugee claim on either trip. When asked about this by the RPD, the Appellant testified that now the difference was that his wife and children were threatened by armed men just as he was leaving Canada after his second trip27. He testified that once his family was threatened, he decided he could not remain in Iraq.

I agree with the RPD that this is not a credible explanation for the Appellant's failure to claim during his first two trips to Canada. If I were to accept the Appellant's allegations, by the time he returned to Canada in XXXX 2016 he had already been threatened by armed men who told him they would kill him and his family. If threats against the Appellant's family really occurred and served as the motivation for him to advance a claim, I find that the Appellant would have made a claim at that time. I agree with the RPD that his failure to do undermines the credibility of his allegation that he and his family were being threatened.

I find that given the inconsistencies and omissions in the Appellant's evidence, he has not credibly established that the events occurred as alleged. I also agree with the RPD that the Appellant's other evidence, including the power of attorney document and rental agreement, do not overcome these credibility findings. I would also note that even taken at face value, these documents only establish a business dispute between the Appellant and Chavy land group. They do not credibly establish that the Appellant has been threatened or faces persecution or a risk to life. Lack of objective evidence about criminal activities noted by the RPD is not contested and is not determinative

The RPD noted that the objective evidence in the National Documentation Package (NDP) did not support the Appellant's argument that Chavy land was involved in criminal activity. The RPD also found that although there was evidence that Chavy land was part of Nalia Corporation, which was headed by Mr. XXXX who was running for office, this did not establish that the Appellant was of interest to him.

The Appellant argues that his new evidence establishes the criminal activity of Chavy Land group. He argues that he faces a serious possibility of persecution and a risk to life on the basis on the threats he received from this group.

For the reasons I have previously outlined, this new evidence has not been accepted on appeal. I agree with the RPD's uncontested analysis of the objective evidence. I find that there is nothing in the objective evidence establishing that Chavy land or Nalia group are involved in criminal activities. I find that Mr. XXXX political aspirations are not determinative as I find that the Appellant has not credibly established he is being threatened by Chavy land group or anyone connected to Mr.

The RPD concluded that the Appellant's residual profile did not establish a claim. The RPD noted that the Appellant listed his religion as Zoroastrian in his BOC and found that the was insufficient objective evidence to find that this would place him at risk. The Appellant does not contest this finding. I also note that the Appellant has not alleged any risk on this basis at the RPD or in his appeal. Nevertheless, I have independently reviewed the objective evidence and I agree with the RPD. While the objective evidence is mixed on the treatment of religious minorities in Iraq, it does not establish that generally Zoroastrians face a serious possibility of persecution or a risk to life.
paragraphs.heading_before: XXXX. The Appellant's religious profile does not establish a claim

paragraphs.text: The RAD dismisses the appeal and confirms the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection, pursuant to section 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).
